entries.title: The Cosmic Reef Nebula
entries.caption: Watercolour interpretation of the Cosmic Reef Nebula, a star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud (a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way) in the constellation Dorado.

entries.title: The Sunflower Galaxy (M63)
entries.caption:
A watercolour interpretation of the Sunflower Galaxy (M63), a spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici.

This galaxy was one of the first in which a spiral structure was identified, and it's considered a "flocculent" galaxy because its arms are not clearly defined. This is contrary to "grand design" spiral galaxies, which I have painted several of before.

entries.title: Centaurus A
entries.caption:
Watercolour interpretation of Centaurus A, the fifth-brightest galaxy in the sky.

This galaxy ejects a powerful relativistic jet, whose inner parts are moving at roughly half the speed of light.

entries.title: The Southern Pinwheel Galaxy (M83)
entries.caption: Watercolour interpretation of M83, the Southern Pinwheel Galaxy, a massive, grand-design spiral galaxy near the constellation border of Hydra and Centaurus. It is at the centre of the M83 galaxy group, next to the Centaurus A galaxy group, and the two are sometimes classified as one larger group.

entries.title: The Black Eye Galaxy (M64)
entries.caption:
Watercolour interpretation of The Black Eye Galaxy (M64).

This spiral galaxy has a dark band of absorbing dust partially in front of its bright nucleus, which gives it its common name.

entries.title: NGC 1501, the Camel's Eye Nebula
entries.caption: A watercolour interpretation of NGC 1501, also known as the Camel's Eye Nebula or the Oyster Nebula. It's a planetary nebula in the constellation Camelopardalis.

entries.title: The Cartwheel Galaxy
entries.caption:
The Cartwheel Galaxy!

It's believed that the Cartwheel Galaxy was once a normal spiral galaxy, but then underwent a face-on collision with a smaller galaxy, causing a powerful gravitational shock wave that gave rise to its now very complicated structure.

entries.caption: The grand-design spiral galaxy M100, sometimes known as the "Mirror Galaxy" due to its similarity to our Milky Way

entries.caption: The Pinwheel Galaxy (M101), a spiral galaxy in the constellation Ursa Major. It is a rather large galaxy, containing around 1 trillion stars.

entries.title: The Antennae Galaxies (NGC 4038/NGC 4039)
entries.caption:
The Antennae Galaxies (NGC 4038/NGC 4039), in the constellation Corvus, are undergoing a galactic collision.

As the galaxies gradually merge, they are also undergoing a period of rapid star formation.

In a few billion years, it's likely that the Milky Way and our neighbouring galaxy, Andromeda, will undergo a similar collision.

entries.title: The Whirlpool Galaxy (M51)
entries.caption:
The Whirlpool Galaxy, M51a, and dwarf galaxy M51b. 

The Whirlpool Galaxy was the first galaxy to be classified as a spiral galaxy. 

M51 is of great interest to astronomers who study the structure of spiral galaxies and how galaxies interact with one other.

entries.title: The Orion Nebula (M42)
entries.caption:
The Orion Nebula (M42).

I usually work on two "identical" paintings simultaneously to make sure I get a good one! But they're never quite identical, and whilst I was happy with both in this case, they have clear differences between them. I felt that the first was more detailed and similar to the original, whilst the second one had a little more depth to it.

entries.title: Watercolour tip: starting a galaxy
entries.caption: Watercolour tip #1: when paining a galaxy or any kind of glowing space object, start by painting a sort of glowing region without worrying at all about the specific shape of the object, or any fine details. This is the beginning of an M82 painting (an early attempt). Detail such as the red "explody bits" are layered on top layer on.

entries.caption: This is M16, the Eagle Nebula, in A2 size (also known as the Pillars of Creation). It is the biggest watercolour painting I have ever created, and was requested by my (very awesome) brother.
